desc:
Given an integer array nums (any order) and two integers lower ≤ upper, count the pairs of positions i < j with lower ≤ nums[i] + nums[j] ≤ upper.

nums = [1, 7, 3, 5, 2], lower = 6, upper = 9
pairs: 1+5=6, 1+7=8, 7+2=9, 3+5=8, 5+2=7
result = 5
hints: Counting pairs with a sum between two bounds is awkward directly. Can you express it using counts of the form “sum at most X”?
The number of pairs with sum in [lower, upper] equals (pairs with sum ≤ upper) minus (pairs with sum ≤ lower - 1).
Sort once. To count pairs with sum ≤ X, put lo at the start and hi at the end: if a[lo] + a[hi] ≤ X add hi - lo and move lo; else move hi.
editorial: Define f(X) = the number of pairs with sum at most X. All pairs with a sum in the range are exactly those counted by f(upper) but not by f(lower - 1), because the sums are integers. So the answer is f(upper) - f(lower - 1).

Compute f on the sorted array with two pointers: when a[lo] + a[hi] ≤ X, element lo pairs with all of lo+1..hi, so add hi - lo and advance lo; otherwise a[hi] is too large for every remaining partner and is dropped. Each call is O(n), so the whole algorithm is O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n).

Binary searching the partner range of every element gives the same answer in O(n log n) too; the two-pointer sweep avoids the logarithm after sorting. The count of pairs fits in 32 bits (at most about 5 × 10<sup>7</sup>).
